destination.title: Periods and special geometry
destination.question: How can periods and special geometry be determined in explicit Calabi–Yau families and near degenerations, and what separate realizability questions arise for formal special geometries?
destination.summary: Explicit period pairing and asymptotic Hodge methods address field-space geometry. Formal physical-versus-motivic realizability remains a separate comparison boundary.

systems: Polynomial deformations of Fermat Calabi–Yau hypersurfaces
Degenerating Calabi–Yau threefold and fourfold settings
Formal special geometries as an alternate comparison setting
targets: Special Kähler potentials and period pairing
Asymptotic periods, couplings and Hodge-theoretic operators
Comparison of physical and motivic realizability
regimes: Asymptotic moduli boundaries, including regimes beyond large complex structure
assumptions: Polynomial deformations do not automatically exhaust all deformation directions
Necessary exponential corrections depend on the quantity being approximated
conventions: Appendix η and ζ are Hodge-theoretic operators
Their finite component formulas are not a physical small-parameter expansion
includes: Method contributions from fourfold operator relations
Weil–Petersson calculations used in qualified normalization shortcuts
excludes: Internal Ricci-flat metric construction inferred from a special Kähler potential
Equality of physical and motivic realizability asserted as a result

evidence.text: Choose Lefschetz thimbles that factor into five one-dimensional contours. Their oscillatory integrals determine a transition matrix T; combine T, the residue pairing and the real structure to eliminate the separate cycle-intersection matrix from the Kähler-potential computation.

evidence.text: Use the Q-invariant Milnor ring RQ = (C[x1,…,x5]/Jac(W0))Q with its residue pairing. Its degree-0,d,2d,3d pieces encode the relevant Hodge grading, while oscillatory integrals identify ring classes with Calabi–Yau periods.
